Melanotan II.overview:
Melanotan II (MT-II) is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It was developed in the 1980s at the University of Arizona as part of efforts to produce a sunless tanning agent, and it was also noticed to affect sexual arousal, which led to the later development of the related compound bremelanotide.

It has never been approved as a medicine in major jurisdictions, yet it is widely sold through gray-market vendors as a injectable or nasal-spray tanning product and is discussed heavily in looksmaxxing communities as a way to darken skin and reduce sunburn risk. Regulators such as the UK MHRA and Australia's TGA have issued warnings against its use, and it should not be confused with the prescription drug afamelanotide.
Melanotan II.mechanism: MT-II is a non-selective agonist at several melanocortin receptors. Activation of MC1R on melanocytes shifts melanin synthesis toward eumelanin and darkens the skin, while activity at MC3R and MC4R in the brain is thought to account for effects on appetite, libido and spontaneous erections. Because it acts systemically rather than only on the skin, its effects are not limited to pigmentation.
Melanotan II.risks: Reported adverse effects include nausea, flushing, fatigue and unwanted erections, and there are case reports of priapism and renal infarction. Case reports and small series describe new or changing moles, including atypical naevi and several melanomas in users, although causation has not been established and users often had other risk factors. Products are unregulated, so purity, sterility and actual content are unverified. Evidence is limited to small early trials, case reports and anecdote; there are no long-term safety data.

Afamelanotide.overview:
Afamelanotide, also called Melanotan I and sold as Scenesse, is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It is delivered as a subcutaneous implant and is approved in the European Union and the United States for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited disorder in which sunlight causes severe pain.

Its relevance to looksmaxxing comes from the fact that it darkens skin, and it is sometimes treated as the legitimate sibling of gray-market Melanotan II. The strong evidence applies only to its approved medical use; it is a prescription product for a specific disease, not a cosmetic tanning option.
Afamelanotide.mechanism: Afamelanotide is a relatively selective agonist at the melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes. Stimulating MC1R increases production of eumelanin, the photoprotective brown-black pigment, and may also support DNA repair and antioxidant responses. In EPP the increased pigmentation and related effects allow patients to tolerate more light exposure before symptoms appear.
Afamelanotide.risks: In clinical trials adverse events were generally mild, with headache, nausea and implant-site reactions most often reported; skin darkening and changes in existing moles are expected effects, so regular skin checks are advised. It is available only by prescription through specialist centres and is costly. It should not be treated as evidence that unregulated melanotan products are safe.

Dihydroxyacetone.overview:
Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is a simple three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in virtually all sunless tanning lotions, sprays and mousses. It is produced commercially by fermentation or chemical conversion of glycerol.

In looksmaxxing it is the standard way to add a tan without UV exposure. It gives a temporary golden-brown colour that fades over several days as the outer skin sheds. It provides little or no sun protection, so it does not replace sunscreen.
Dihydroxyacetone.mechanism: DHA reacts with free amino groups of proteins and amino acids in the stratum corneum through the Maillard reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. The colour is therefore a surface stain rather than a change in melanin production, and it fades as the keratinised cells exfoliate.
Dihydroxyacetone.risks: Topical use is considered low risk and DHA is a permitted colour additive for external application in the US. Reviews note it should not be ingested or inhaled, so spray-booth use needs eye, mouth and nose protection, and that long-term and inhalation safety data are limited. Skin irritation or contact allergy is uncommon. A bigger practical risk is false confidence about sun protection, since the tan does not shield against UV.

scholarly.title: Properties and safety of topical dihydroxyacetone in sunless tanning products: A review

Canthaxanthin.overview:
Canthaxanthin is an orange-red carotenoid found in some bacteria, algae, fungi and animals such as flamingos and certain fish. It is used as a colour additive in animal feed, for example to tint salmon and egg yolks.

In the 1980s it was sold in high-dose oral "tanning pills" that deposited pigment in the skin to give an orange-brown tint. This was not a real tan and offered no reliable UV protection, and the products were later restricted or warned against by regulators in several countries.
Canthaxanthin.mechanism: When taken at high doses over time the fat-soluble pigment accumulates in subcutaneous fat and skin, giving a diffuse orange coloration, a process distinct from melanin production. The same lipid-soluble pigment can also collect in other tissues, including the retina, where it forms the crystalline deposits seen in users.
Canthaxanthin.risks: High cumulative intake of tanning-pill doses has been associated with canthaxanthin crystalline retinopathy, in which glittering yellow crystals appear around the macula; visual function is often preserved but deposits can persist for years. Other reported problems include gastrointestinal upset, hives and rare liver or blood effects. In the US the FDA has not approved it for tanning, so use for that purpose is unapproved and not recommended.

scholarly.title: The Extent of Retinal Involvement of Canthaxanthin Crystalline Retinopathy Demonstrated by Multimodal Imaging

Beta-carotene.overview:
Beta-carotene is a yellow-orange carotenoid pigment found in carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens, and it is a dietary precursor of vitamin A. It is sold as a supplement and used in some sunless-tan and skin-glow products.

In appearance circles it is used to add a warm, golden-yellow tint to the skin. Small human trials suggest that sustained intake raises skin yellowness and that observers can rate the resulting faces as healthier or more attractive, mainly in lightly pigmented skin.
Beta-carotene.mechanism: After absorption with dietary fat, beta-carotene circulates in lipoproteins and is deposited in the skin, particularly in the stratum corneum and subcutaneous fat. The deposited pigment adds a yellow-orange hue to the skin's reflectance. Some is converted to retinol in the body, and it also has antioxidant activity in tissues.
Beta-carotene.risks: Very high intake can cause carotenemia, a harmless but visible orange discolouration that fades after intake is reduced. More importantly, large randomized trials in smokers and people exposed to asbestos found that high-dose beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer risk, so it is not advisable for these groups. The cosmetic effect is modest and variable and is weaker in darker, sun-exposed skin.

Lycopene.overview:
Lycopene is the red carotenoid pigment that gives tomatoes, watermelon and pink grapefruit their colour. It is consumed through food, especially cooked tomato products, and as a supplement.

In skincare it is promoted as an internal photoprotective antioxidant. Intervention trials suggest small reductions in UV-induced redness and some markers of photodamage, but the effects are modest and lycopene does not replace sunscreen.
Lycopene.mechanism: Lycopene is a highly lipophilic molecule that accumulates in skin and is an efficient quencher of singlet oxygen and other reactive oxygen species. By limiting UV-driven oxidative damage and downstream inflammatory and matrix-degrading signals, it is thought to blunt part of the sunburn response. Absorption improves when it is eaten with fat and after heat processing.
Lycopene.risks: Dietary and supplement doses are generally well tolerated. Very high intake can cause lycopenemia, a harmless orange tint to the skin that resolves after reducing intake. Many trials are small and often use tomato paste or industry-supplied extracts, so findings should be read cautiously.

scholarly.title: The effect of tomato and lycopene on clinical characteristics and molecular markers of UV-induced skin deterioration: a systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention trials
scholarly.source: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition (hosted by Lycored, a supplier)

scholarly.title: Carotenoids and protection against solar UV radiation

Astaxanthin.overview:
Astaxanthin is a red-pink xanthophyll carotenoid made by microalgae such as Haematococcus pluvialis and responsible for the colour of salmon, shrimp and flamingos. It is sold as a dietary supplement, typically derived from algae.

In looksmaxxing and skincare it is used for skin hydration, elasticity and defence against UV damage. Systematic reviews find modest improvements in moisture and elasticity in small trials, with less consistent effects on wrinkles.
Astaxanthin.mechanism: Astaxanthin is a potent lipid-soluble antioxidant that spans cell membranes and quenches reactive oxygen species, and in cell studies it dampens UV-induced inflammatory signalling and collagen-degrading enzymes. Whether these effects translate into meaningful clinical change depends on the trials, which are mostly short.
Astaxanthin.risks: Supplements are generally well tolerated at studied doses, with occasional mild gastrointestinal effects and, at high intake, a reddish skin tint. Safety in pregnancy and long-term use is not well established. Most trials are small, many are industry-funded, and several enrolled mainly healthy Japanese women, limiting how far results generalise.

scholarly.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Astaxanthin on Human Skin Ageing
Effects of Astaxanthin Supplementation on Skin Health: A Systematic Review of Clinical Studies

Polypodium leucotomos.overview:
Polypodium leucotomos is a tropical fern native to Central and South America whose leaf extract is sold as an oral supplement, for example under the Fernblock and Heliocare names. It has a long history in traditional medicine and has been studied in dermatology for UV-related skin reactions.

In the appearance space it is used as an "internal sunscreen" adjunct to reduce sunburn, photoaging and pigmentation. Clinical studies suggest modest benefit, but it is not a substitute for sunscreen.
Polypodium leucotomos.mechanism: The extract is rich in phenolic compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. In studies it reduces UV-induced DNA damage and inflammatory mediators, limits generation of reactive oxygen species, and may support Langerhans cell function in skin. It does not absorb UV like a sunscreen filter.
Polypodium leucotomos.risks: Oral extract is generally well tolerated, with occasional mild gastrointestinal upset, headache or itching; serious adverse effects have not been reported in published reviews. Evidence comes from small trials with varied formulations, so supplements that do not specify the studied extract may not be equivalent.

Glutathione.overview:
Glutathione is a tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine and glycine and is the main small-molecule antioxidant inside most cells. It is available as oral, sublingual, topical and intravenous products.

It is heavily marketed, particularly in parts of Asia, for skin lightening, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing forums for the same purpose. Controlled evidence of visible whitening is limited and inconsistent, and professional bodies have warned against intravenous use for this purpose.
Glutathione.mechanism: Proposed lightening mechanisms include inhibition of tyrosinase, the key melanin-producing enzyme, and a shift from darker eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin through cysteine availability. Oral glutathione is poorly absorbed and largely broken down in the gut, so it is unclear how much reaches skin melanocytes.
Glutathione.risks: Intravenous use outside medical indications has been linked to rashes and severe allergic or skin reactions, and some regulators, including the Philippine FDA and dermatology societies, have issued warnings. Injectable products from informal sources carry contamination and dosing risks. Any lightening seen in small studies tends to be mild and may reverse after stopping.

L-Cysteine.overview:
L-cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that the body can make from methionine and that is also supplied by protein-rich foods. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing, and its acetylated form N-acetylcysteine is a well-known medicine.

In skin-tone discussions it is mentioned as a glutathione precursor and because cysteine participates in melanin pathways. Evidence that it lightens skin is weak and mostly indirect.
L-Cysteine.mechanism: Cysteine is the rate-limiting amino acid for glutathione synthesis. Its availability is also thought to steer melanocytes toward pheomelanin, the lighter pigment, rather than eumelanin. Whether supplemental doses meaningfully change visible pigmentation in people is unproven.
L-Cysteine.risks: Typical dietary and low-dose supplemental intake is generally tolerated, with possible gastrointestinal upset. High doses can cause nausea and other effects, and people with cystinuria or on certain medications should avoid it without advice. Products marketed for lightening are not approved for that use.

Teriparatide.overview:
Teriparatide is a recombinant fragment of human parathyroid hormone (residues 1-34) used as a daily injection to treat severe osteoporosis. Unlike most osteoporosis drugs, which slow bone loss, it stimulates new bone formation.

It appears in looksmaxxing talk because of speculation that bone-building drugs could enhance jaw or facial bone. There is no evidence for cosmetic skeletal change in healthy adults, and its approval covers osteoporosis only.
Teriparatide.mechanism: Intermittent exposure to PTH fragments stimulates osteoblasts through the PTH1 receptor, increasing bone formation more than resorption in the short term. Continuous exposure instead promotes bone breakdown, which is why the treatment pattern matters. Effects are largest in trabecular bone such as the spine.
Teriparatide.risks: Possible effects include nausea, dizziness, leg cramps and raised blood calcium. Osteosarcoma was seen in high-dose rodent studies, which led to a former boxed warning and treatment duration limits. It is prescription-only, expensive and not appropriate for people with certain bone conditions or prior radiation. It is not an approved or evidence-based cosmetic treatment.

Romosozumab.overview:
Romosozumab (Evenity) is a monoclonal antibody given by monthly injection for up to a year to treat osteoporosis in people at high fracture risk. It was approved in Japan, the United States and Europe around 2019.

It is sometimes mentioned in looksmaxxing contexts as a bone-builder, but its approval covers osteoporosis only, and there is no evidence that it changes facial structure in healthy people.
Romosozumab.mechanism: Romosozumab binds sclerostin, a protein produced by osteocytes that inhibits Wnt signalling in bone-forming cells. Blocking it increases bone formation and reduces bone resorption, giving a dual effect that raises bone density rapidly, especially in the spine and hip.
Romosozumab.risks: It carries a boxed warning for heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death, and is not given to people with a recent event of this kind. Other concerns include low blood calcium, injection-site reactions, and rare osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures. It is a prescription drug requiring clinical supervision and is not a cosmetic treatment.

Vitamin K2.overview:
Vitamin K2 is a group of fat-soluble compounds called menaquinones, most commonly sold as MK-4 and MK-7, found in fermented foods such as natto, some cheeses and animal products. It is popular in bone and "facial structure" supplement stacks alongside vitamin D and calcium.

Its role is to activate calcium-binding proteins including osteocalcin. Trial results on bone density and fractures are mixed, with the strongest signals coming from high-dose MK-4 studies in Japan, and no evidence that it alters facial bone in healthy adults.
Vitamin K2.mechanism: Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which modifies osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein so they can bind calcium. Carboxylated osteocalcin helps incorporate calcium into bone matrix, and matrix Gla protein is thought to limit calcification of soft tissue such as arteries. MK-7 persists in circulation longer than MK-4.
Vitamin K2.risks: Supplements are generally well tolerated, and no upper limit has been set. It can interfere with warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, so people on anticoagulants should seek medical advice. Claims about cardiovascular or bone benefits are stronger in marketing than in controlled trials.

Calcium.overview:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body, with the great majority stored in bones and teeth, where it provides rigidity. It is obtained from dairy, fortified foods, leafy greens and supplements.

Adequate intake supports bone mineralisation and peak bone mass, which matters for the skeleton overall. Supplementation helps mainly when dietary intake is low; extra calcium does not reshape facial bone in people who already get enough.
Calcium.mechanism: Calcium is deposited as hydroxyapatite in the bone matrix, while a small circulating fraction signals muscle contraction, nerve transmission and clotting. Blood levels are tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin, with bone acting as a reservoir that is drawn on when intake falls short.
Calcium.risks: Excess intake from supplements can cause constipation, kidney stones and hypercalcaemia, and some studies have raised questions about cardiovascular effects of high-dose supplements. Dietary sources are preferred where possible, and calcium can interact with certain antibiotics and thyroid medicines.

Magnesium.overview:
Magnesium is an essential mineral involved in hundreds of enzyme reactions, including energy metabolism, muscle and nerve function and bone structure. About half of the body's magnesium is held in bone.

It is a common supplement for sleep, cramps and general bone health. The strongest evidence is for correcting a deficiency; beyond that, claims about cosmetic or structural benefit are weak.
Magnesium.mechanism: Magnesium acts as a cofactor for ATP-dependent enzymes and influences calcium handling, parathyroid hormone secretion and vitamin D activation, all of which affect bone turnover. It is also incorporated into the bone mineral surface and acts as a reservoir.
Magnesium.risks: Supplements, especially magnesium oxide and citrate, can cause diarrhoea and abdominal cramping, and people with kidney impairment can accumulate it to dangerous levels. It can interact with some antibiotics and bisphosphonates. Dietary intake from nuts, seeds, legumes and greens is generally safe.

Boron.overview:
Boron is a trace element found in fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes and is sold as a supplement, typically as boric acid, calcium fructoborate or boron citrate. It is not classed as an essential nutrient in humans, although it is considered beneficial.

In bone-focused circles it is used for its possible effects on mineral and sex-hormone metabolism. Human evidence is limited to small studies, and it should not be taken to enhance facial bone structure.
Boron.mechanism: Proposed effects include influencing the metabolism of calcium, magnesium and vitamin D, and modulating steroid hormone levels and inflammatory markers. The exact mechanisms in humans are not well established.
Boron.risks: Normal food intake is safe, but high supplemental doses can cause nausea, diarrhoea and other toxicity, and an upper intake level has been set by authorities. Concerns include reproductive and developmental effects at high exposures, so it should be avoided in pregnancy without advice.

Caffeine (topical).overview:
Topical caffeine is included in many under-eye creams and serums intended to reduce puffiness and dark circles. It is the same xanthine alkaloid found in coffee and tea, used here at low concentrations in a cosmetic base.

The effect is cosmetic and temporary. Some small studies show reduced swelling and improved appearance, but the evidence is limited and often uses short follow-up and company-run designs.
Caffeine (topical).mechanism: Caffeine is a vasoconstrictor that narrows small vessels, which may reduce visible blood pooling and fluid in the thin periorbital skin. It may also act as an antioxidant and may promote lipolysis and drainage in tissue, although penetration through skin is modest and effects are short-lived.
Caffeine (topical).risks: Topical use is usually well tolerated, with occasional irritation or allergy. Contact with the eyes should be avoided. Absorbed amounts are small, but product claims are often stronger than the evidence, and the effect does not address structural causes of eye bags such as fat prolapse.

Hesperidin.overview:
Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside concentrated in the peel of citrus fruits. It is sold as a supplement, often combined with diosmin in products used for chronic venous insufficiency and haemorrhoids.

In the context of facial puffiness and dark circles it is occasionally added to creams and supplements for its effects on small blood vessels. Evidence for periorbital use specifically is limited, and most clinical data concern venous disorders.
Hesperidin.mechanism: Hesperidin and its aglycone hesperetin are thought to improve vascular tone and capillary resistance, reduce microvascular permeability and dampen inflammation through antioxidant pathways. Oral bioavailability is low and depends on gut bacteria releasing the active aglycone.
Hesperidin.risks: Generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal upset, headache or rash occasionally reported. It is recognised as safe as a food ingredient, but interactions with some medications that are metabolised by the liver are possible, and evidence for cosmetic claims is weak.

Dandelion extract.overview:
Dandelion extract comes from the leaves or roots of Taraxacum officinale and is traditionally used as a mild herbal diuretic and digestive aid. It is sold as tea, capsules and tinctures.

In the appearance space it is marketed for "water weight" and facial bloating. Human evidence for a meaningful diuretic effect is very limited, so the claimed benefit for face depuffing is largely unsupported.
Dandelion extract.mechanism: Dandelion leaf contains potassium and compounds that may promote modest urine output in animal studies, and the root contains inulin and sesquiterpene lactones. A small pilot study reported a short-lived increase in urination, but this is not strong evidence of a clinically significant effect.
Dandelion extract.risks: Allergic reactions can occur in people sensitive to the daisy family (Asteraceae), including ragweed. It may interact with diuretics, lithium, anticoagulants and some antibiotics, and could raise potassium in susceptible people. Quality of herbal products varies.

Potassium.overview:
Potassium is an essential electrolyte that governs fluid balance, nerve signalling and muscle contraction, and is abundant in fruit, vegetables, legumes and dairy. Most people get it from food rather than supplements.

In depuffing discussions it is mentioned because a higher potassium-to-sodium balance supports normal fluid regulation. Fixing a high-sodium diet is more relevant than taking pills, and evidence for facial de-bloating from potassium supplements is thin.
Potassium.mechanism: Potassium is the main intracellular cation. It works with sodium and the kidney to set extracellular fluid volume, and higher potassium intake promotes sodium excretion and lowers blood pressure. The face may look less puffy when overall fluid retention falls, though many causes of facial puffiness are unrelated to electrolytes.
Potassium.risks: Over-the-counter potassium supplements are limited in dose because excess can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia and heart rhythm problems, particularly in people with kidney disease or taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics. Cosmetic use should not override medical advice.

Furosemide.overview:
Furosemide (Lasix) is a potent loop diuretic used to treat fluid overload from heart failure, kidney disease and cirrhosis, and sometimes high blood pressure. It is prescription-only in nearly all countries.

It turns up in appearance and bodybuilding circles as a way to drop water weight quickly. For face slimming it is both dangerous and ineffective, since any change reflects temporary fluid loss, not fat or bone.
Furosemide.mechanism: Furosemide blocks the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, so the kidney excretes more sodium, chloride, potassium and water. Onset is quick and the effect is strong, which makes electrolyte disturbances easy to cause.
Furosemide.risks: Misuse can cause dehydration, low potassium, sodium and magnesium, cramps, dizziness, kidney injury, hearing damage and dangerous heart rhythms. It can interact with many drugs and is contraindicated in anuria and sulfonamide hypersensitivity. Use without medical supervision for cosmetic purposes is unsafe and is prohibited in many sports.
